debugInfo.title: Debugging
debugInfo.intro: These tools help you understand what an application does, instruction by instruction, like a computer debugger.
debugInfo.code: the disassembled code, breakpoints, stepping, registers and the call stack.
debugInfo.points: all breakpoints (conditional if needed) and watchpoints, which can be disabled without losing them.
debugInfo.watch: which instruction reads or writes a memory range.
debugInfo.console: the same actions from the keyboard, with GDB-style commands.
debugInfo.profile: where the application spends its time (the most visited functions and addresses).
debugInfo.calls: the application's calls to the calculator's system, with their arguments.
debugInfo.limit1: Nwasabi emulates the processor, not the whole calculator: the system (Epsilon), the peripherals and the real chip's access times are replaced by simplified versions. You debug your code against this simulated system, not against the exact chip.
debugInfo.limit2: Function names come from the symbols of the .nwa file: without them only addresses are shown. The call stack is estimated and is not always exact.
debugInfo.limit3: There are no exception handlers: a fault stops the application. The fault registers are nevertheless filled like the real processor does.
debugInfo.limit4: Setting breakpoints or watchpoints slows the emulation down.

profile.title: Execution profile
profile.help: Regularly records the instruction being executed: the functions and addresses that come up most often are where the application spends its time. Recording goes on until you stop it.
profile.waiting: No samples yet: an application that spends its time waiting (screen, keyboard) runs too few instructions to be profiled.

snapshot.title: Compare two moments
snapshot.help: Takes a photo of the RAM, then compare it later with the current state: you see, by byte range, what the application changed in between. To find one particular variable the value search is more direct; this shows everything that moved.

svclog.show: Show the instruction in the debugger
svclog.argsNote: The four registers are shown as they are: not all of them are arguments, depending on the call. Values are in hexadecimal.

fault.title: Application fault

kinds.unimplemented: Instruction not handled by the emulator

bus.unmapped: The application tried a {access} of {size} byte(s) at {address}, where there is no memory. This is typically a null or corrupted pointer.
bus.accessdenied: The application tried a {access} of {size} byte(s) at {address}, an area where that access is forbidden (writing to flash, executing data…).
bus.exclusiveunsupported: The application used an exclusive-access instruction (ldrex, strex) on shared memory: the real calculator refuses it too.

fault.unimplemented: The emulator cannot (yet) run the instruction {word}. If the application works on a real calculator, this is a limit of the emulator.

usage.UndefinedInstruction: The application ran an undefined instruction (udf): most often it jumped into data.
usage.InvalidState: The application jumped to an even address: a Cortex-M only runs Thumb, whose jump addresses are odd.
usage.Unaligned: The application made an unaligned memory access with an instruction that forbids it (ldm, stm, ldrd, strd).
usage.other: The application did something the processor forbids.

fault.breakpoint: The application ran a break instruction (bkpt #{imm}).
fault.unknownSvc: The application made system call {number}, which the simulated kernel does not know.
fault.waitForInterrupt: The application waits for an interrupt that nothing can trigger.
fault.note: The application is stopped: you can examine its memory and registers, or restart it.

faultregs.bfar: Address of the memory access that failed (read or write).

bits.iaccviol: The processor tried to run code in an area where that is forbidden.
bits.daccviol: Data access forbidden at this address (for example writing to flash).
bits.mmarvalid: MMFAR holds the address of the forbidden access.
bits.ibuserr: The code to run could not be read: there is no memory at this address.
bits.preciserr: Data access to an address with no memory; the faulting instruction is known exactly.
bits.bfarvalid: BFAR holds the address of the faulting access.
bits.invstate: Jump to an even address: a Cortex-M only runs Thumb.
bits.unaligned: Unaligned access with an instruction that forbids it.
bits.forced: The fault was escalated to a HardFault, for lack of a dedicated handler.

points.conditionHelp: With a condition, the application only stops if the register satisfies it (unsigned values; “&”: at least one bit in common).

trace.cpuHelp: The processor is an ARM Cortex-M7. Its registers are small 32-bit memories inside the chip, read at regular intervals (those that just changed are highlighted).

flag.N: N (negative): the last result is negative, its top bit is 1.
flag.Z: Z (zero): the last result is zero, or a comparison found two equal values.
flag.C: C (carry): an addition overflowed, or a subtraction did not borrow; used for unsigned comparisons.
flag.V: V (overflow): the result does not fit in a signed 32-bit integer.
flag.Q: Q (saturation): a saturating instruction reached its limit; the flag stays set until cleared.

trace.svcHelp: The application's calls to the kernel (svc instruction), from most to least frequent ({frames} frames).

regInfo.args: Arguments and result of a function (r0 to r3); a function may overwrite them freely.
regInfo.saved: Local variables: a function must restore them as it found them.
regInfo.r12: Temporary scratch register (IP), freely overwritten by calls.
regInfo.sp: Stack pointer (r13): top of the stack, where local variables and return addresses live.
regInfo.lr: Link register (r14): where to resume when the current function returns.
regInfo.pc: Program counter (r15): address of the instruction being executed.
regInfo.xpsr: Status register: flags N Z C V Q, the Thumb bit and the current exception number.
regInfo.fpscr: Floating-point control and status: rounding mode and error flags.

trace.flagsHelp: Four bits of xpsr sum up the result of the last operation and drive conditional branches; the ones that are set are colored.

svcInfo.24: Tells whether an event has a defined meaning.

svcInfo.55: Repeat count of a held key.

svcInfo.130: Writes text to the standard output.

The browser may ask your permission to keep them durably. They stay on this computer, are shared by everything that runs on this site, and you can erase them or change your mind at any time in the Settings tab.

scan.title: Memory value search
scan.help: This search finds the memory addresses that hold a given value. The first search keeps every matching address; each next search keeps, among them, only those whose new value satisfies the chosen comparison (exact value, changed, increased…). Repeating it after each change of the value in the application isolates the address that holds it. The retained addresses can be added to the list to be read continuously, modified or held at a value.
scan.noApp: Load an application to search its memory.
scan.aligned: Addresses aligned to the type size only (faster, and almost always what you want)
scan.showing: The first {n} results are shown: narrow the search.
scan.truncated: Too many results: the search stopped at {n} addresses.
scan.listHelp: Values are read continuously. Typing a value and pressing Enter writes it to memory, in the format of the address's type; “Hold” keeps writing the value so that it stays unchanged.
scan.listEmpty: The list is empty: add addresses from the results.
scan.badValue: “{text}” is not a valid value for this type ({type}).

quick.title: Quick save
quick.help: One slot in this browser, no file: Ctrl + S saves the emulation state (application, memory, files, processor), Ctrl + O reloads it.
quick.saveHint: Saves the state in this browser (the simulation pauses for a moment).
quick.loadHint: Replaces the emulation with the saved state and resumes it.
